newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway puts welfare at top of strategic thinking.
newsitem.headline: Norway puts welfare at top of strategic thinking.

text.p: Oil-rich Norway presented its strategic economic plan for the next four years on Friday and in the best Scandinavian tradition said it would give priority to its social welfare system while preparing for ebbing oil revenues.

The Long Term Programme 1998-2001 is designed to meet the challenges of medium-term stability in the economy and lower oil income, set against rising pension costs and potentially stronger environmental constraints.

Launching the plan, Planning Minister Bendik Rugaas said the framework aimed to keep wage growth low and prevent long-term unemployment, while improving economic growth and enhancing competitiveness of the non-oil economy.
"This (low wage and costs growth) is one premise for full employment, which again is necessary to secure the welfare state," Rugaas told a news conference.
"It is one line in our work for high employment, full nursery schools, flexible working hours and efforts to stimulate elderly employees to continue to work."

The minority Labour government, which faces an election in September, said priority would be given to welfare services for old people, health care, nursey schools, adult training, development aid, culture and information technology.
Fiscal policy for the next four years would concentrate
on not harming the mainland economy by burdening it with inflation and to keep public expenditure at a level which is sustainable when oil revenues decline, a government statement said.
Monetary policy would be oriented at keeping the crown stable against European currencies.

The Norwegian economy has been in a strong cyclical upswing for more than three years. The oil and gas-rich Scandinavian land of just 4.3 million people is the second largest crude exporter after Saudi Arabia and is one of the few European countries to show a budget surplus.
"Growth, job creation, unemployment, inflation and external and fiscal balances are among the best in the industrial world," the statement said.

The budget surplus in 1996 amounted to 45.7 billion crowns ($6.6 billion) and was forecast to reach 55.4 billion crowns in 1997. All the money is ploughed into the state's Petroleum Fund for investment overseas to be used to pay future pension costs.

In its latest plan, the government said the state's net cash flow from petroleum activities was estimated to reach a peak of 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2001, and then gradually decline.
The Petroleum Fund was expected to exceed 400 billion crowns by 2001, it said.

It forecast overall GDP to grow by an average 2.75 percent per year to 2001 and by 0.75 percent per annum from 2001 to 2005. Mainland GDP -- which excludes the oil and gas sector -- was seen rising by an annual rate of two percent to 2005.
Consumer prices were projected to rise annually by 2.5 percent up to 2005. The unemployment rate was forecast to decline to four percent in 2001 from 4.9 percent in 1996.
